meta.subject: math
meta.title: Odd and Even Numbers: Pairs, Doubles and Counting by 2s
meta.description: A free Grade 2 lesson and worksheet on odd and even numbers: making pairs with objects up to 20, counting by 2s, writing even numbers as doubles and using the ones digit. Includes a timed lesson plan, a seven-activity worksheet, an editable Word version and an answer key.
meta.overview: Students find out whether a group of objects is odd or even by making pairs: if one is left over, the number is odd. They count by 2s, write even numbers as the sum of two equal addends (such as 14 = 7 + 7), and discover that the ones digit tells us whether any number is odd or even. Every math answer in the pack is calculated by the generator and checked automatically.
learning_objectives: Decide whether a group of up to 20 objects is odd or even by making pairs or counting by 2s.
Write an even number as the sum of two equal addends (a double), such as 12 = 6 + 6.
Use the ones digit to tell whether a 2-digit number is odd or even.
how_to_use: Teach the lesson with counters or cubes following the lesson plan.
Do activities 1–3 together, then let students finish activities 4–7 on their own.
Check the work with the answer key; use activity 7 to hear each student's reasoning.
meta.skills_practiced: Number sense, counting by 2s, doubles, reasoning and explaining
activity_ideas: Partner check: call out a number of students; they try to make pairs and decide if the number is odd or even.
Stand or sit: say a number; students stand up for even and stay seated for odd.
Sock sort: give groups a pile of socks and ask them to find out if there is an odd or even number.
meta.teacher_tips: Let students touch and move counters before they use the ones digit rule. Ask "Is anyone left without a partner?" so the idea of odd and even stays concrete.
meta.differentiation_notes: Support: give students counters for activities 1 and 3 and a hundred chart for activity 4. Challenge: ask students to explain what happens when you add two odd numbers.
meta.assessment_notes: Activities 1–6 check pairing, counting by 2s, doubles and the ones digit (answer key included). Activity 7 shows whether students can explain their reasoning.

vocabulary.definition: a number you can split into pairs with none left over
vocabulary.example: 8 is even: 4 pairs and none left over.

vocabulary.definition: a number that has one left over when you make pairs
vocabulary.example: 7 is odd: 3 pairs and 1 left over.
I have a pair of socks.

vocabulary.definition: groups that have the same number
the last digit of a number

materials: Counters or cubes (about 20 per pair of students)

stages.name: Warm-up
steps: Ask the class to stand up and find a partner. Ask: "Is anyone left without a partner?"
Count the students. Say: "When everyone has a partner, the number is even. When one person is left over, the number is odd."

stages.name: Presentation
steps: Show 6 counters and make pairs: 3 pairs, none left over, so 6 is even. Show 7 counters: 3 pairs and 1 left over, so 7 is odd.
Split 6 counters into two equal groups and write 6 = 3 + 3. Explain that every even number can be written as a double.
Count by 2s to 20 and write the numbers on the board. Ask: "What do you notice about the ones digits?" (0, 2, 4, 6, 8)

stages.name: Guided practice
steps: Do activity 1 together: circle pairs of pictures and decide odd or even.
Students complete activities 2 and 3 with a partner, using counters to check the doubles.

stages.name: Independent practice
steps: Students complete activities 4, 5 and 6 on their own.
Ask individual students: "How do you know 58 is even?" Look for the ones digit or a double (29 + 29).

stages.name: Wrap-up
steps: Stand or sit game: say a number; students stand for even and stay seated for odd.
Students answer activity 7 to explain their thinking (finish for homework if needed).

support: Use counters for activities 1 and 3 and a hundred chart for activity 4.
Start with numbers up to 10 before moving to numbers up to 20.
challenge: Add two odd numbers several times (3 + 5, 7 + 9). Is the answer odd or even? Explain why.
Find a number between 40 and 60 that is even and has a ones digit greater than 5.

lesson_plan.assessment: Check activities 1–6 with the answer key. In activity 7, look for answers that use pairs, equal groups or the ones digit to explain.

sections.title: Make pairs
sections.instructions: Circle the pictures in pairs. If one is left over, the number is odd. Write odd or even.

sections.title: Count by 2s
sections.instructions: Count by 2s. Write the missing number.

sections.title: Doubles
sections.instructions: Even numbers split into two equal groups. Write each number as a double. Example: 8 = 4 + 4

sections.title: Look at the ones digit
sections.instructions: Look at the ones digit. Write odd or even.

sections.title: Sort the numbers
sections.instructions: Write each number in the odd or even column.

sections.title: True or false?
sections.instructions: Read each sentence. Circle True or False.

items.statement: If you can make pairs with none left over, the number is even.
The number after an even number is always even.
Two equal groups of 7 make 14, so 14 is even.

sections.title: Explain your thinking
sections.instructions: Write your answer on the lines.

items.q: There are 13 children. Can every child have a partner? Explain.
items.answer: No. 13 is odd: 6 pairs make 12, so 1 child is left without a partner.

items.q: Is 30 odd or even? How do you know?
items.answer: Even. Its ones digit is 0, and 30 = 15 + 15 (two equal groups).
